title: How to Walk Into Any Interview Prepared
excerpt: Talent gets you shortlisted but preparation gets you hired. Here is a structured way to research any company, master the STAR method, ask smart questions back, handle video calls, and answer the salary question with confidence.
content:
A graduate named Tunde once sat before a three person panel at a bank in Victoria Island, Lagos. He had the grades. His CV had beaten hundreds of others to get him into that room. Then came the opening question: “What do you know about us?” He went blank. He knew the bank’s name and the colour of its logo. The interview was effectively over within four minutes.

Tunde did not lack talent. He treated the interview as a test of talent, when it is really a test of preparation. Talent gets you shortlisted. Preparation gets you hired. If your CV is not yet doing its job, start with our guide to the CV that gets you interviews. Then come back, and let’s take the questions candidates fear most, one at a time.

The questions candidates fear, answered

“What do you know about us?”

The goal is simple: know more than the interviewer expects. LinkedIn’s research on candidate experience found that 71 percent of candidates research a company before they even apply, so skimming the website is not preparation, it is the baseline. You need to go one layer deeper.

Spend one focused evening on four things: the company’s own words (website, blog, latest annual results if it is listed), recent news such as a funding round or an expansion, your interviewers’ LinkedIn profiles, and the market: main competitors, obvious challenges. Then compress it into two sentences you could say out loud: “You’ve grown from a Nairobi payments startup into three East African markets in four years, and the big question in your space seems to be agent network costs. That is partly why this operations role interests me.” A candidate who can say that calmly is instantly memorable.

One more shortcut: if anyone in your circle works there, or used to, ask them what the company is wrestling with right now. That is exactly the kind of insight the hidden job market runs on.

“Tell me about a time you...”

Behavioural questions feel unpredictable. They are not. Every skill in the job description, from “works well under pressure” to “attention to detail”, is a question waiting to happen. Prepare a story for each one, structured with the STAR method recommended by the UK National Careers Service: Situation, Task, Action, Result.

Here is a worked example. The question: “Tell me about a time you solved a problem under pressure.” A weak answer says, “I stay calm during busy periods and get things done.” It sounds fine and proves nothing. Now watch STAR work, in the voice of a candidate interviewing for an operations role in Accra:

Situation: “During my national service year at a logistics company in Accra, our delivery tracking system crashed on the busiest Friday of the Christmas season. Drivers were calling in with nowhere to log their jobs.”
Task: “I was the most junior person on the desk, but my supervisor asked me to keep deliveries moving until IT restored the system.”
Action: “I set up a simple shared form we could all update from our phones, briefed our six drivers by voice note within ten minutes, and logged every delivery manually with timestamps so nothing would be lost when the system came back.”
Result: “We completed all but three of that day’s ninety deliveries. My supervisor kept the backup form as standard practice, and I learned that in a crisis, a simple tool everyone understands beats a clever one nobody can use.”

Notice the shape: brief scene, clear responsibility, specific actions, measurable result, one line of learning. Prepare five or six stories like this from work, school, community roles, or volunteering, and practise each aloud in about ninety seconds. In the room, you are not inventing answers. You are choosing from a shelf.

“Do you have any questions for us?”

Never say no. Harvard Business Review’s guide to smart questions to ask in a job interview notes that this moment does two jobs at once: it keeps proving your interest, and it helps you decide whether you actually want the role. Prepare three. Good ones: “What would you expect me to achieve in my first 90 days?”, which also sets you up to deliver once you start, as we cover in your first 90 days. “What is the biggest challenge the team faces right now?” “What separates people who do well here from those who just do okay?” Avoid anything a quick search could answer, and save leave and perks for after there is an offer.

“What if it is a video interview and something goes wrong?”

Virtual interviews are now routine, especially for remote and international roles, so treat the technology as part of the interview itself. The National Careers Service’s video interview guidance covers the basics: test your microphone and software in advance, log in early, put the camera at eye level, light your face, and pause briefly after each question so you do not talk over the interviewer on a delayed connection.

Then add the realities many of us know too well. Charge your laptop in case the power goes. Load a backup data bundle and know how to hotspot from your phone. Tell everyone at home when your call is. If the connection drops anyway, do not spiral: rejoin, apologise once, and continue. Interviewers remember how you handled the glitch far longer than the glitch itself. If you are chasing remote roles with employers abroad, our guide to earning globally while living locally goes deeper.

“What are your salary expectations?”

The question that makes palms sweat: go too low and you lose money, go too high and you fear losing the job. Writing for Harvard Business Review, Amy Gallo’s advice on answering the salary expectations question starts with research. Ask two or three people in your network what the realistic band is for this role in this city. Check ranges in similar postings. Ask any recruiter you speak with.

Then give a researched range, not a single number, and anchor toward its upper part: “From what I understand of similar roles in Lagos, a range of X to Y seems fair, and I am open to discussing the full package.” If you truly found no data, ask politely whether there is a budgeted band; many employers have one. Remember the package is more than the number: transport allowance, health cover, pension, and training all count. Just never pluck a low figure out of fear. You are not begging for a favour. You are pricing a service.

Your pre-interview checklist

The night before any interview, run through this list:

  • Re-read the job description and your own application. Anything on your CV is fair game.
  • Write two sentences on the company: what it does, where it is going, why you want in.
  • Look up your interviewers on LinkedIn and note one genuine point of connection with each.
  • Prepare five or six STAR stories matched to the skills in the job description, and say them out loud once.
  • Prepare three questions to ask back.
  • Decide your salary range and the evidence behind it.
  • Confirm the time (and time zone), the venue or link, and your interviewers’ names and titles.
  • For video calls: test your setup, charge everything, load backup data, and secure a quiet, well lit spot.
  • Plan your outfit and your journey with a generous traffic buffer, then sleep properly.

Preparation is not about being perfect on the day. It is about knowing you have done everything within your control, so your energy goes into the conversation instead of the panic. Do this every time, even for interviews that do not end in offers, and each becomes rehearsal for the one that will. Walk in prepared, and you will walk out taller either way.
